In [[mathematics]], '''duality theory for distributive lattices'''  provides three different (but closely related) representations of [[distributive lattice|bounded distributive lattices]] via [[Priestley space]]s, [[spectral space]]s, and [[pairwise Stone space]]s. This duality, which is originally also due to [[Marshall H. Stone]],<ref> Stone (1938)</ref> generalizes the well-known [[Stone duality]] between [[Stone space]]s and [[Boolean algebra (structure)|Boolean algebra]]s.

Let {{math|''L''}} be a bounded distributive lattice, and let {{math|''X''}} denote the [[set (mathematics)|set]] of [[Ideal (order theory)|prime filters]] of {{math|''L''}}. For each {{math|''a'' <small>∈</small> ''L''}}, let {{math|''φ''<sub>+</sub>(''a'') {{=}} {''x''<small>∈</small> ''X'' : ''a'' ∈ ''x''{{)}}}}. Then {{math|(''X'',''τ''<sub>+</sub>)}} is a spectral space,<ref>Stone (1938), Johnstone (1982)</ref> where the [[topological space#Definitions|topology]] {{math|''τ''<sub>+</sub>}} on {{math|''X''}} is generated by {{math| {''φ''<sub>+</sub>(''a'') : ''a'' <small>∈</small> ''L''{{)}}}}. The spectral space {{math|(''X'', ''τ''<sub>+</sub>)}} is called the ''prime spectrum'' of {{math|''L''}}.

The [[map (mathematics)|map]] {{math|''φ''<sub>+</sub>}} is a lattice [[isomorphism]] from {{math|''L''}} onto the lattice of all [[compact set|compact]] [[open set|open]] subsets of {{math|(''X'',''τ''<sub>+</sub>)}}. In fact, each spectral space is [[homeomorphism|homeomorphic]] to the prime spectrum of some bounded distributive lattice.<ref>Stone (1938), Johnstone (1982)</ref>

Similarly, if {{math|''φ''<sub>&minus;</sub>(''a'') {{=}} {''x''<small>∈</small> ''X'' : ''a'' ∉ ''x''} }} and {{math|''τ''<sub>&minus;</sub>}} denotes the topology generated by {{math|{''φ''<sub>&minus;</sub>(''a'') : ''a''<small>∈</small> ''L''{{)}}}}, then {{math|(''X'',''τ''<sub>&minus;</sub>)}} is also a spectral space. Moreover, {{math|(''X'',''τ''<sub>+</sub>,''τ''<sub>&minus;</sub>)}} is a [[pairwise Stone space]]. The pairwise Stone space {{math|(''X'',''τ''<sub>+</sub>,''τ''<sub>&minus;</sub>)}} is called the ''[[bitopological space|bitopological]] dual'' of {{math|''L''}}. Each pairwise Stone space is bi-homeomorphic to the bitopological dual of some bounded distributive lattice.<ref>Bezhanishvili et al. (2010)</ref>

Finally, let {{math|≤}} be set-theoretic inclusion on the set of prime filters of {{math|''L''}} and let {{math|''τ'' {{=}} ''τ''<sub>+</sub><small>&or;</small> ''τ''<sub>&minus;</sub>}}. Then {{math|(''X'',''τ'',≤)}} is a [[Priestley space]]. Moreover, {{math|''φ''<sub>+</sub>}} is a lattice isomorphism from {{math|''L''}} onto the lattice of all [[clopen set|clopen]] [[up-set]]s of {{math|(''X'',''τ'',≤)}}. The Priestley space {{math|(''X'',''τ'',≤)}} is called the ''Priestley dual'' of {{math|''L''}}. Each Priestley space is isomorphic to the Priestley dual of some bounded distributive lattice.<ref>Priestley (1970)</ref>

Let '''Dist''' denote the category of bounded distributive lattices and bounded lattice [[homomorphisms]]. Then the above three representations of bounded distributive lattices can be extended to [[Equivalence of categories|dual equivalence]]s<ref>Bezhanishvili et al. (2010)</ref> between '''Dist''' and the categories '''Spec''', '''PStone''', and  '''Pries''' of spectral spaces with spectral maps, of pairwise Stone spaces with bi-continuous maps, and of Priestley spaces with Priestley morphisms, respectively:

[[Image:DL Duality.png|thumb|center|alt=Spec, Pries and Pstone are isomorphic, all three are dually equivalent to Dist|Duality for bounded distributive lattices]]

Thus, there are three equivalent ways of representing bounded distributive lattices. Each one has its own motivation and advantages, but ultimately they all serve the same purpose of providing better understanding of bounded distributive lattices.
